question: In REALM, how are the top‑k documents retrieved efficiently when approximating the marginal probability p(y | x)?
answer: REALM finds the top-k documents efficiently using Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) on the inner-product relevance score f(x, z) = Embedinput(x)⊤Embeddoc(z), since the ordering of documents under p(z|x) matches the ordering under this relevance score, and MIPS runs in sub-linear time and space with respect to corpus size.
title: REALM: Retrieval-Augmented Language Model Pre-Training
evidence: Even with this approximation, we still need an efficient way to find the top k documents. Note that the ordering of documents under p(z | x) is the same as under the relevance score f(x, z) = Embedinput(x)⊤Embeddoc(z), which is an inner product. Thus, we can employ Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) algorithms to find the approximate top k documents, using running time and storage space that scale sub-linearly with the number of documents (Ram & Gray, 2012; Shrivastava & Li, 2014; Shen et al., 2015).

question: In the Fusion-in-Decoder model for open-domain QA, why does the reading component process each retrieved passage independently from the others?

title: Leveraging Passage Retrieval with Generative Models for Open Domain Question Answering
evidence: More precisely, each retrieved passage and its title are concatenated with the question, and processed independently from other passages by the encoder.

question: What is the Jeopardy question generation task introduced in the Retrieval‑Augmented Generation paper?
answer: It is a non‑QA evaluation where the model must generate Jeopardy‑style questions—precise factual statements that require guessing an answer entity—from given answer entities, serving as a challenging knowledge‑intensive generation task.
title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
evidence:
3.3 Jeopardy Question Generation

To evaluate RAG’s generation abilities in a non-QA setting, we study open-domain question generation. Rather than use questions from standard open-domain QA tasks, which typically consist of short, simple questions, we propose the more demanding task of generating Jeopardy questions. Jeopardy is an unusual format that consists of trying to guess an entity from a fact about that entity.

TFR = p(EMpLM(y|[q,x]) = 0|EMpLM(y|q) = 1)

FFR = p(EMpLM(y|[q,x]) = 1|EMpLM(y|q) = 0),

question: How does the CausalFusion preprocessing pipeline extract high‑confidence cause‑effect pairs for CDF‑RAG?
answer: CausalFusion combines a finetuned causal classifier with LLM‑based validation: it annotates candidate argument spans in sentences, passes them through a BERT‑based encoder trained on the UniCausal framework to predict whether a causal relation exists, and uses the binary judgments to filter for high‑quality causal pairs.
title: CDF-RAG: Causal Dynamic Feedback for Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation
evidence: This component combines finetuned causal classification with LLM-based validation to extract high-confidence cause-effect pairs from each dataset. Specifically, we build on the UniCausal (Tan et al., 2023) framework and focus on the Causal Pair Classification task. Sentences from each dataset are annotated with candidate argument spans (<ARG0> and <ARG1>), which are passed through a BERT-based encoder trained to predict whether a causal relationship exists between them. The model outputs binary judgments that filter candidate pairs down to high-quality causal candidates.

question: How does the Parametric retrieval-augmented generation (Parametric RAG) method incorporate external knowledge into a large language model?

This approach not only saves online computational costs by eliminating the need to inject multiple documents into the LLMs’ input context

question: In PA‑RAG's instruction fine‑tuning stage, how are the prompt documents selected for each question?
answer: They first retrieve the top‑100 documents with the RAG retriever, keep the "golden" ones that contain the short answer, and then choose up to five of those golden documents as prompt documents, making sure all short answers appear in the prompts.
title: PA-RAG: RAG Alignment via Multi-Perspective Preference Optimization
evidence: We use the RAG retriever to retrieve the top 100 most relevant documents from the retrieval corpus, and then filter to retain the golden documents that contain the short answer. Subsequently, we select up to five documents from all the golden documents as prompt documents, ensuring that all short answers are included in the prompt documents.

question: Why does SimGRAG align query text with KG subgraphs using Graph Semantic Distance (GSD) instead of approaches like KAPING, G‑retriever, KG‑GPT, or KELP?
answer: Because GSD provides a plug‑and‑play, scalable way to match queries to subgraphs while avoiding the drawbacks of other methods: KAPING struggles with multi‑hop queries, G‑retriever cannot guarantee concise subgraphs, KG‑GPT depends on an LLM to select relations which hurts scalability, and KELP requires a trained path‑selection model.
title: SimGRAG: Leveraging Similar Subgraphs for Knowledge Graphs Driven Retrieval-Augmented Generation
evidence: Specifically, (i) KAPING (Baek et al., 2023) employs query text to directly retrieve isolated triples using their semantic embedding similarity, which struggles with multi-hop queries as the query embedding captures excessive information. (ii) G-retriever (He et al., 2024) uses query text embeddings to retrieve similar entities and relations, then extracts a connected components in KG, which potentially cannot guarantee the best conciseness of the retrieved subgraphs. (iii) KG- GPT (Kim et al., 2023a) segments the query into sub-sentences but depends on the LLM to decide relations in KG that can match each sub-sentence, compromising scalability as the number of candidate relations increases. (iv) KELP (Liu et al., 2024) trains a path selection model to identify paths that align with the query text, lacking the plug-andplay usability even on human-understandable KGs.

question: Why did the creators design AsthmaBot to be both multi‑modal and multi‑lingual?

title: AsthmaBot: Multi-modal, Multi-Lingual Retrieval Augmented Generation For Asthma Patient Support
evidence:
However, existing RAG systems only produce textual information and are not multi-modal in addition LLMs suffer from language biases, which limits the quality of information that they generate in languages other than English.

In this work, we introduce AsthmaBot, an automated asthma medical support multi-lingual, multi-modal RAG system.

question: In DuetRAG, what are the two methods used to implement the referee model Mj for assessing answer credibility?

title: DuetRAG: Collaborative Retrieval-Augmented Generation
evidence: Our work on the referee model Mj, responsible for assessing the credibility of answers and generating the final result, involves the design and implementation of two methods: classification and summarization. The classification method is inspired by the training approach of CLIP. It constructs data q, a based on the training set Ttrain to train Mj, achieving semantic alignment between questions and answers. The summarization method utilizes the inherent reasoning and summarization capabilities of the large language model itself.

question: In the MedRGB benchmark's robustness test, where retrieved documents contain misinformation, which model had the highest factual-error detection rate despite performing worst overall?
answer: GPT‑3.5 achieved the highest factual error detection rate while being the worst‑performing model.
title: Comprehensive and Practical Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems for Medical Question Answering
evidence: Interestingly, GPT-3.5 has the highest factual errors detection rate while being the worst-performing model.

question: What three properties does RAGAS score when evaluating a RAG pipeline?
answer: Faithfulness (the answer is grounded in the retrieved context), answer relevance (the answer addresses the question that was asked), and context relevance (the retrieved context is focused, with as little irrelevant information as possible).
title: Ragas: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
evidence: We focus in particular three quality aspects, which we argue are of central importance. First, Faithfulness refers to the idea that the answer should be grounded in the given context. This is important to avoid hallucinations, and to ensure that the retrieved context can act as a justification for the generated answer. Indeed, RAG systems are often used in applications where the factual consistency of the generated text w.r.t. the grounded sources is highly important, e.g. in domains such as law, where information is constantly evolving. Second, Answer Relevance refers to the idea that the generated answer should address the actual question that was provided. Finally, Context Relevance refers to the idea that the retrieved context should be focused, containing as little irrelevant information as possible.

question: In MultiFinRAG, how does Gemma 3's accuracy compare with Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct, and what explains the difference?
answer: Gemma 3 reaches 66.7% accuracy versus 42.9% for Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct, because Gemma 3 describes the images and graphs in the files in more detail.
title: MultiFinRAG: An Optimized Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Framework for Financial Question Answering
evidence: In contrast, MultiFinRAG with Gemma 3 achieves higher accuracy (66.7%) compared to MultiFinRAG with Llama-3.2-11B-Vision- Instruct (42.9%), indicating that Gemma 3 is more adept at describing images and graphs in the files in a detailed and comprehensive manner.

question: Does neutralizing sarcasm in already-neutral text hurt RAG reading comprehension, and what gains are reported on NQ and on sarcasm-injected datasets?
answer: No. It gives a 0.9% boost on NQ and an average gain of 3.6% on the sarcasm-injected datasets.
title: Emotional RAG LLMs: Reading Comprehension for the Open Internet
evidence: Importantly, applying neutralization to already-neutral text does not harm performance, producing a 0.9% boost on the NQ dataset and an average gain of 3.6% on sarcasminjected datasets.

question: In a query-aware knowledge-graph fusion approach to RAG, how many Recall@10 points does fine-tuning add on SQuAD for bge_base versus bge_large?
answer: Fine-tuning improves Recall@10 by 9.27 points for bge_base and by 12.82 points for bge_large.
title: A Query-Aware Multi-Path Knowledge Graph Fusion Approach for Enhancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Large Language Models
evidence: For example, on the SQuAD dataset, fine-tuning the bge_base model results in a 9.27point increase in Recall@10, while the bge_large model achieves an even greater improvement of 12.82 points.
